guides.title: Conservatism
guides.summary: The conservative political tradition: its origins in Burke's response to the French Revolution, its core arguments about tradition, human nature, institutions and law, its major national variants from Britain and America to Christian democracy and beyond, and the criticisms it faces.

sections.heading: What Conservatism Is
sections.body:
Conservatism is one of the three or four political traditions that have shaped the modern world, and it is
the hardest of them to define. Liberalism can be summarised by a commitment to individual liberty, socialism
by a commitment to collective ownership or material equality. Conservatism resists that treatment, because
what it seeks to conserve differs from country to country and century to century. A conservative in
nineteenth-century France defended monarchy and an established church; a conservative in twenty-first
century America defends a written constitution produced by a revolution and a market economy that
constantly dissolves inherited arrangements. These are not the same programme, and yet the label is not
arbitrary.

What unites them is better described as a disposition and a set of characteristic arguments than as a
doctrine. The philosopher Michael Oakeshott put it as a preference for the familiar to the unknown, the
tried to the untried, the actual to the possible, the limited to the unbounded. The historian and political
theorist Russell Kirk, cataloguing what he called the conservative mind in 1953, listed belief in a
transcendent moral order, affection for the variety and mystery of traditional life, conviction that
civilised society requires orders and classes, a link between property and freedom, faith in custom over
abstract design, and recognition that change and prudence must be kept in balance. Not all conservatives
accept all of these, and some accept almost none, which tells you something important about the category.

Three distinctions clear away most confusion at the outset. First, conservatism is not simply the defence of
whatever exists. Conservatives have frequently been radicals of restoration, seeking to undo changes they
regard as recent errors, and in a country whose recent past is socialist a conservative may be an advocate
of sweeping market reform. Second, conservatism is not identical with the political right, which also
contains libertarians, nationalists, and movements conservatives have historically opposed with some
ferocity. Third, small-c conservatism as a temperament, meaning caution about change, is distinct from
capital-C Conservatism as an organised political movement, and a person may have plenty of one and none of
the other.

The tradition matters for reasons beyond party politics. Its central intellectual claim, that societies
contain accumulated knowledge which no individual reformer fully understands and which reform can destroy
inadvertently, is a serious argument about the limits of human knowledge that has been developed
independently in economics, in complexity theory, and in engineering. Its central political claim, that
legitimacy and stability depend on continuity and on institutions people actually feel loyalty toward,
addresses a real problem that any regime must solve. Understanding conservatism means taking those claims
seriously enough to see where they are strong, and where their critics have landed genuine blows.

sections.heading: Burke and the Origins of the Modern Tradition
sections.body:
Conservatism as a self-conscious body of thought is usually dated to a single book: Reflections on the
Revolution in France, published by the Irish-born British parliamentarian Edmund Burke in November 1790.
The dating is somewhat artificial, since arguments for tradition and hierarchy are as old as political
writing, but the label is defensible. Burke wrote at the moment when revolutionary politics made the
defence of inherited order into a distinct position rather than an unexamined assumption.

The circumstances matter. Burke was a Whig, a member of the party of parliamentary supremacy and limited
monarchy. He had spent his career opposing established power: he defended the American colonists against
the Crown in the 1770s, campaigned for years against the abuses of the East India Company in Bengal, and
argued for relief of Irish Catholic disabilities. He was not a reflexive defender of authority, which is
why his hostility to the French Revolution surprised his allies and delighted his opponents. Thomas Paine's
Rights of Man, published in 1791, was written as a direct reply, and Mary Wollstonecraft's Vindication of
the Rights of Men preceded it by weeks.

Burke's objection was not to change but to a particular method of change. The French, he argued, had
attempted to rebuild a society from abstract first principles, the rights of man derived by reason, sweeping
away institutions that had grown over centuries because they could not be justified in those terms. His
counter-argument had several strands. Society is a partnership, and in his most quoted formulation a
partnership not only between those living but between those who are living, those who are dead, and those
who are to be born. Institutions embody the accumulated practical wisdom of many generations, most of it
never articulated, so the fact that a custom cannot be defended in theory is weak evidence that it is
useless. Individuals are limited: the private stock of reason in each person is small, and they do well to
draw on the general bank and capital of nations and of ages. Abstraction is dangerous because human affairs
are complex and consequences are unpredictable, and reform should therefore proceed cautiously, repairing
rather than demolishing.

He also made a prediction that did much for his reputation. A revolution that destroyed all traditional
authority, he wrote, would end not in liberty but in the rule of the army, with some popular general seizing
power. The Terror began in 1793 and Napoleon Bonaparte took power in the coup of 18 Brumaire in 1799.

Modern readers should note what the argument does not establish. It shows that inherited institutions may
encode information and that rapid reconstruction is risky. It does not show that any particular institution
is good, and Burke's critics pointed out from the start that the accumulated wisdom of ages had also
produced slavery, torture and hereditary privilege, all of which required deliberate abolition against
exactly this kind of caution.

sections.heading: The Core Dispositions
sections.body:
Beneath the many national variants lie a handful of recurring habits of mind. They are not axioms from
which conclusions are deduced; they are tendencies that push in a direction, and they can conflict with one
another, which is why conservatives argue among themselves as vigorously as they argue with anyone else.

The first is a presumption in favour of the existing. Where a liberal or socialist asks whether an
arrangement can be justified, the conservative asks who bears the burden of proof and answers that it falls
on the person proposing the change. This is not a claim that what exists is good. It is a claim about
epistemic asymmetry: we have direct evidence about how present arrangements work, since they are working in
front of us, and only conjecture about how proposed arrangements would work. The essayist G. K. Chesterton
gave the classic illustration in 1929 with the image of a fence across a road. The reformer proposes to
clear it away; the conservative replies that until you can tell me why it was put there, I will not let you
remove it, and that once you can explain its purpose you may well be right to remove it. The principle is
epistemic, not obstructive.

The second is prudence, understood in the classical sense as practical judgement about particular
circumstances rather than as timidity. Burke insisted that circumstances give to every political principle
its distinguishing colour and discriminating effect, so that the same measure may be right in one country
and catastrophic in another. This produces a characteristic conservative distrust of policy exported
wholesale between contexts.

The third is scepticism about abstract reason applied to human affairs. Society is treated as more like an
organism or an ecosystem than a machine, with countless interdependencies its participants do not fully
understand, so interventions have consequences their designers did not intend. This intuition was later
given technical form in economics, most influentially by Friedrich Hayek's argument about dispersed
knowledge, and it has independent parallels in ecology and in software engineering, where the risks of
rewriting a complex working system from scratch are well documented.

The fourth is a preference for the concrete and particular over the universal. Conservatives tend to speak
of this country, this town, this family, this church, and to treat loyalty to specific people and places as
morally basic rather than as a lesser version of loyalty to humanity. Burke's phrase for the small local
associations that form character, the little platoon we belong to in society, captures it.

The fifth is an acceptance of hierarchy and inequality as natural or at least unavoidable, though the
strength of this varies enormously and it is the element most sharply contested by conservatives influenced
by market liberalism.

sections.heading: Human Nature and the Limits of Reason
sections.body:
Almost every distinctive conservative political conclusion traces back to a view of what human beings are
like. Where progressive traditions have often held that people are naturally cooperative or at least
malleable, and that vice is largely produced by bad institutions, conservatism holds that human nature is
fixed in its essentials, mixed in its qualities, and not perfectible by political means.

In religious versions this is stated as the doctrine of original sin or of fallen human nature: people are
capable of great good but permanently prone to selfishness, cruelty, self-deception and short-sightedness,
and no arrangement of institutions will eliminate that. Secular conservatives make a parallel argument from
history and, more recently, from evolutionary psychology and behavioural science, pointing to the
regularity with which utopian projects have produced tyranny and to well-documented cognitive limitations
in reasoning about complex systems. Thomas Sowell, in A Conflict of Visions in 1987, framed the whole left
and right division as a disagreement between what he called the constrained vision, which sees human
limitations as permanent facts to be worked around through incentives and institutions, and the unconstrained
vision, which sees them as remediable through the right arrangements and sufficient enlightenment.

Two political consequences follow directly. The first concerns the design of institutions. If people are
permanently self-interested and fallible, institutions must be built to function despite that rather than
to depend on virtue, which favours divided power, checks and balances, adversarial procedures, secret
ballots, independent courts and the rule of law over discretion. James Madison's formulation in Federalist
51, that if men were angels no government would be necessary and that the great difficulty is first to
enable the government to control the governed and then to oblige it to control itself, is the canonical
statement, and it is a strikingly conservative sentence in an otherwise liberal document.

The second consequence concerns ambition. If reformers cannot foresee consequences, then the scale of
intervention should be limited and reversibility valued. The conservative preference for incremental change
is not merely a taste for slowness; it is a strategy for error correction, since small changes produce
detectable failures that can be undone while large simultaneous changes produce failures that cannot be
disentangled or reversed.

The critics' reply deserves fair statement, because it is substantial. If human nature sets hard limits,
those limits have repeatedly turned out to lie much further out than conservatives claimed. The abolition of
slavery, the extension of the franchise to those without property and then to women, the creation of mass
public education, the establishment of universal healthcare in many countries, and the extension of legal
equality on racial and sexual grounds were all opposed at the time by conservative arguments about human
nature, social order and unintended consequences, and all were achieved without the predicted collapse.
That record is a genuine problem for strong versions of the argument.

sections.heading: Institutions, Civil Society and Subsidiarity
sections.body:
Conservatism has always paid unusual attention to the layer of social life that sits between the individual
and the state: families, congregations, guilds, unions, clubs, charities, universities, neighbourhood
associations and local government. In the conservative account these are not sentimental extras but the
load-bearing structure of a society, and their health is the real measure of its condition.

The argument runs in several directions at once. Descriptively, these bodies do most of the work of raising
children, transmitting norms, caring for the old and sick, resolving disputes and generating the trust that
makes commerce and public life possible, and they do it without coercion and largely without cost to the
treasury. Formatively, they are where character is made: Alexis de Tocqueville, whose Democracy in America
appeared in two volumes in 1835 and 1840, argued that Americans' habit of forming voluntary associations
was what prevented democratic individualism from leaving citizens isolated and defenceless before a
centralised power. Protectively, they stand between the individual and the state, so that a person with a
family, a church, a union and a town has multiple sources of support and identity and is harder to coerce.

From this follows one of conservatism's most portable ideas, subsidiarity: matters should be handled by the
smallest, lowest or least centralised authority competent to address them. The principle was given its
classic formulation in Catholic social teaching, in Pope Pius XI's encyclical Quadragesimo Anno of 1931,
which held it a grave evil to assign to a greater and higher association what lesser and subordinate
organisations can do. It was later written into European Union law by the Maastricht Treaty of 1992, where
it functions, at least in principle, as a limit on the centralisation of decisions. Federalism in the United
States and in Germany embodies a comparable idea in constitutional form.

The conservative anxiety attached to this analysis is that both the state and the market can hollow out
these intermediate bodies. When government assumes functions that families and voluntary associations used
to perform, the argument goes, those associations atrophy from disuse, and citizens come to relate to a
distant bureaucracy instead of to neighbours. Robert Nisbet made this case at length in The Quest for
Community in 1953, arguing that the growth of the modern state had left individuals atomised and therefore
vulnerable to mass movements. Later conservatives have levelled a parallel charge at commerce, arguing that
market mobility, advertising and the reorganisation of work dissolve local attachments just as effectively.

Empirically the picture is mixed and contested. Robert Putnam's Bowling Alone, published in 2000,
documented substantial declines in American associational membership and civic participation over several
decades, which conservatives read as confirmation. Critics note that the causes Putnam identified were
mostly television, suburbanisation, generational change and time pressure rather than welfare provision, and
that the Nordic countries combine expansive welfare states with unusually high levels of associational
membership and social trust, which is difficult to reconcile with the crowding-out thesis in its strong form.

sections.heading: Property, Prescription and the Rule of Law
sections.body:
Conservative political thought has consistently linked liberty to property, and both to legal continuity.
The connection is not primarily economic. It is about the conditions under which a person can be
independent of power, and about how legal certainty is generated.

The property argument holds that a person who owns something, land, a house, tools, a business, a pension,
has a base from which to resist pressure, a stake in the stability of the order that protects it, and a
horizon that extends beyond the present. Widespread ownership therefore produces citizens with an interest
in prudent government. This reasoning is why many conservative traditions have favoured broad distribution
of property rather than mere protection of existing holdings. The distributist writers Hilaire Belloc and
G. K. Chesterton argued in the early twentieth century that both large-scale capitalism and socialism
concentrated control and left ordinary people propertyless and dependent, and that the remedy was to spread
ownership widely. British Conservative governments after 1979 promoted a property-owning democracy through
council house sales on comparable reasoning.

The legal argument centres on the concept of prescription, one of Burke's key terms. A prescriptive right
is one whose legitimacy derives from long, undisturbed possession and usage rather than from any original
title that could be produced. Burke's claim was that this is the strongest basis for property and for
constitutions alike, precisely because it does not depend on a founding moment whose validity can be
disputed. English common law formalised the intuition in doctrines of adverse possession and easement by
long use, on the practical ground that after enough time, settled expectations matter more than the original
paperwork, which has usually been lost.

From this flows a distinctive conservative reading of the rule of law. Law should be general, applying to
everyone including officials; knowable in advance, so that people can plan; stable, so that today's
arrangements are not overturned tomorrow; and administered by independent courts rather than by
discretionary official judgement. The emphasis on predictability is the conservative note. Friedrich Hayek's
The Road to Serfdom in 1944 and The Constitution of Liberty in 1960 gave the fullest modern statement,
arguing that a legal framework of stable general rules is what allows people to use knowledge only they
possess, and that discretionary administration destroys that even when it is well intentioned.

Common law itself is often held up as the paradigm case of a conservative institution. It was not designed
by anyone. It accumulated case by case as judges resolved concrete disputes, with each decision constrained
by precedent through the doctrine of stare decisis, so that the system encodes the results of many thousands
of practical judgements. Critics point out that this same evolved system also encoded, and defended for a
long time, coverture, racial exclusion and other doctrines nobody now defends, and that the corrective in
each case came from legislation or constitutional amendment rather than from within the tradition.

sections.heading: Conservative Constitutionalism and Judicial Philosophy
sections.body:
Because conservatism prizes legal continuity, it has generated a distinctive body of thought about
constitutions and the role of judges. The central preoccupation is the allocation of authority: who gets to
decide contested questions, and by what warrant. Conservatives have generally argued that this authority
should sit with legislatures accountable to voters or with the amendment procedures written into
constitutions, rather than with courts, which are unelected and reason from general principles.

Judicial restraint is the older form of the position. It holds that courts should strike down legislation
only where the conflict with the constitutional text is clear, and should otherwise defer to the elected
branches. In the United States this was for decades a conservative response to the Supreme Court's
expansion of rights doctrine from the 1950s onward, though restraint has switched sides more than once in
American history: the same argument was made by progressives against the Court that struck down New Deal
legislation in the 1930s, which is a useful reminder that judicial philosophies often track whose ox is
being gored.

Originalism, which largely displaced restraint as the leading conservative approach in America from the
1980s, is a theory of interpretation rather than deference. Its claim is that a constitutional provision
means what it meant when it was ratified, and that judges are bound by that meaning until it is changed by
amendment. Early versions sought the original intent of the drafters; the dominant modern version, developed
by scholars including Antonin Scalia and later Randy Barnett and Lawrence Solum, seeks the original public
meaning of the words to a competent reader at the time, which avoids the difficulty of aggregating the
intentions of many people. Textualism is the corresponding approach to statutes: interpret the words
enacted, not the purposes attributed to legislators afterwards. The Federalist Society, founded in 1982,
was the principal institutional vehicle for spreading both.

The strongest argument for originalism is about constraint and legitimacy. If a text can be given whatever
meaning current judges find reasonable, then judicial review becomes an unelected veto exercised by lawyers,
and the written constitution ceases to bind. The strongest arguments against it are that original meaning is
frequently indeterminate on the questions that actually reach appellate courts, that the historical research
required is beyond the competence of most judges and produces contested results, that applying
eighteenth-century meanings to technologies and social arrangements the drafters never imagined requires
judgement the theory cannot supply, and that in practice the results have tracked the political preferences
of its adherents closely enough to raise doubts about how constraining it really is.

Outside the United States the debate takes different forms, because most constitutions are younger and
courts have different roles. The German Basic Law's eternity clause, protecting certain provisions from
amendment altogether, and the British tradition of parliamentary sovereignty, under which no court may
strike down an Act of Parliament, represent two very different answers to the same underlying question.

sections.heading: Continental Reaction and Throne-and-Altar Conservatism
sections.body:
The conservatism that developed on the European continent after 1789 was considerably harsher than Burke's,
and it is important not to read the gentler Anglo-American tradition backward onto it. Where Burke defended
a mixed constitution with a strong parliament and had supported the American colonists, the continental
counter-revolutionaries defended absolute monarchy, an established church and a corporate social order, and
regarded the entire Enlightenment as an error to be reversed.

Joseph de Maistre, a Savoyard nobleman who spent years as ambassador to the Russian court, is the most
formidable of them. In Considerations on France of 1797 and Soirées de Saint-Pétersbourg published in 1821
he argued that political constitutions cannot be written but only grow, that sovereignty must be absolute
and unquestionable to be effective, that the Pope's authority is the necessary check on temporal power, and
that social order rests ultimately on force and on a shared sacred framework. His observation that he had
seen Frenchmen, Italians and Russians but had never met Man in general was a direct attack on the abstract
universal subject of revolutionary rights talk. His writing is bleak, sometimes shockingly so; his
meditation on the executioner as the hidden foundation of social order has troubled readers for two
centuries and has been read both as grim realism and as something closer to relish.

Louis de Bonald developed a parallel case, arguing that society is prior to the individual and that language
itself, being social and inherited, demonstrates that no one reasons from a genuinely individual starting
point. Juan Donoso Cortés in Spain made the theological case most explicitly, holding that every political
question is at bottom a theological one.

Institutionally this tradition found expression in the settlement Klemens von Metternich engineered at the
Congress of Vienna in 1814 and 1815, which sought to restore legitimate dynasties, contain nationalism and
suppress revolutionary movements across Europe through coordinated action. The system held, with revolts and
adjustments, until the revolutions of 1848 broke it.

Two points of judgement matter for a reader today. First, this tradition is genuinely a different animal
from Burkean conservatism, and treating them as one obscures more than it explains: Burke's argument is
epistemic and can support gradual reform, while de Maistre's is theological and authoritarian and cannot.
Second, the continental counter-revolutionary strand had a real and unhappy influence on later
authoritarian movements. Historians disagree sharply about how direct that line is, and it would be a
serious distortion to treat conservatism generally as proto-fascist, given that conservative parties and
churches also produced substantial resistance to fascism. But the intellectual resources for authoritarian
politics were present in this branch, and honest accounts of the tradition say so.

sections.heading: British Conservatism: Toryism to One Nation
sections.body:
The British Conservative Party is the longest continuously governing party in the democratic world, and its
history is the best available case study in how a conservative movement adapts to changes it originally
opposed. Its origin lies in the Tory faction of the late seventeenth century, which supported royal
prerogative and the established Church of England against the Whigs. The modern party is conventionally
dated to Sir Robert Peel's Tamworth Manifesto of 1834, which accepted the Great Reform Act of 1832 that
Tories had bitterly resisted and committed the party to the correction of proved abuses and the redress of
real grievances while resisting change for its own sake. That formula, accepting an accomplished reform and
then defending the new settlement, has been repeated so often that it constitutes the party's characteristic
method.

Benjamin Disraeli gave the tradition its most distinctive doctrine. In his novel Sybil of 1845, subtitled
The Two Nations, he described rich and poor as two nations between whom there is no intercourse and no
sympathy, and argued that the governing class had a duty of care toward the poor precisely because of its
privileges. As Prime Minister from 1874 he legislated accordingly, with public health and housing
legislation and the legalisation of peaceful picketing. This paternalist strand, later called One Nation
conservatism, treats society as an organic whole with reciprocal obligations between classes, and it
distinguishes British conservatism sharply from purely market-liberal versions. It also explains why the
Conservative Party accepted and administered the welfare state and the National Health Service after 1951
rather than dismantling them, a period sometimes called the postwar consensus.

The other pole is represented by Margaret Thatcher, Prime Minister from 1979 to 1990, whose governments
privatised state-owned industries, curtailed union power, cut direct taxes, sold council houses to their
tenants and rejected the postwar consensus explicitly. Thatcherism is often described as conservative but
its content was substantially classical liberal, and it was disruptive of settled communities in a way
that troubled traditionalists within her own party. She herself once remarked, correcting an aide who
described her as a Tory, that she was a nineteenth-century liberal. The tension between the paternalist
and market strands has structured Conservative politics ever since.

The British case illustrates a general point about conservative parties: their survival depends on
absorbing changes they opposed. Catholic emancipation in 1829, the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846 which
split the party, successive extensions of the franchise, the welfare state, decolonisation, and eventually
the legalisation of same-sex marriage under a Conservative government in 2013 were all resisted and then
accepted, and in each case the accepted settlement became something the party subsequently defended. Whether
this shows admirable pragmatism or an absence of principle is one of the standing arguments about
conservatism, and both readings have serious defenders.

sections.heading: Free Markets and the Liberal Strand
sections.body:
Much of what is called conservatism in the English-speaking world today is, in intellectual ancestry,
classical liberalism: a commitment to free markets, limited government, low taxation and individual
economic liberty. This is a genuine confusion worth untangling, because the marriage between market
liberalism and traditional conservatism is neither ancient nor obviously stable.

The core arguments are those of Adam Smith, whose Wealth of Nations appeared in 1776, and of the twentieth
century Austrian school. Hayek's most influential contribution, set out in his 1945 article on the use of
knowledge in society, was that the economic problem is not the allocation of known resources but the use of
knowledge that exists only in dispersed fragments, held by particular people in particular circumstances and
often not articulable. Prices aggregate that dispersed knowledge into a single signal that coordinates
millions of decisions without anyone needing to comprehend the whole. Central planning fails not because
planners are stupid or wicked but because the information they would need does not exist in any collectable
form. This is a striking parallel to the Burkean claim about accumulated social knowledge, and it is why
the two traditions found each other.

Yet Hayek himself denied he was a conservative, and the essay in which he did so is essential to
understanding the tension. Why I Am Not a Conservative, appended to The Constitution of Liberty in 1960,
argued that conservatism has no independent direction of its own, being merely a brake on movement; that it
is too willing to use state authority to enforce traditional morality; that it is hostile to
internationalism and prone to nationalism; and that it fears change as such, whereas the liberal welcomes
change that is spontaneous rather than imposed. He proposed the label Old Whig for his own position.

The substantive tension is real and shows up constantly in practice. Markets are the most powerful engine of
social disruption ever devised. They dissolve traditional occupations, empty out towns whose industry moves
elsewhere, draw women and then both parents into paid work outside the home, reward mobility over rootedness,
and treat inherited practices as costs to be optimised away. A conservative who values stable communities,
settled family arrangements and continuity of place has reason to be uneasy about exactly the forces a
market liberal celebrates. Karl Polanyi's The Great Transformation of 1944, though written from the left,
made this argument with a force many traditionalist conservatives have since acknowledged.

The historical resolution, at least in the United States, was fusionism, a term associated with the
National Review editor Frank Meyer in the 1960s. Its claim was that free markets and traditional virtue are
complements rather than rivals, since virtue must be freely chosen to count as virtue, and that both camps
faced a common enemy in communism. The alliance held for roughly four decades. Its subsequent fraying, once
the common enemy disappeared, is a large part of the story of conservative politics after 1991.

sections.heading: American Conservatism and Fusionism
sections.body:
American conservatism is a distinctive case because the tradition it seeks to conserve is itself a liberal
one. The United States has no feudal past, no established church, no hereditary aristocracy and no ancien
régime; its founding document asserts natural rights and the consent of the governed. Louis Hartz argued in
The Liberal Tradition in America in 1955 that this makes American conservatism necessarily a defence of
Lockean liberalism, and that European-style conservatism could never take root. The claim is contested but
it identifies something real: American conservatives typically appeal to the Constitution and the founding,
which is to say to a revolutionary settlement, as the thing to be preserved.

Before the Second World War the American right was fragmented, combining business opposition to the New
Deal, agrarian and Southern traditionalism, and a strong non-interventionist strand. The movement acquired
coherence in the 1950s through a set of institutions and books. Russell Kirk's The Conservative Mind in 1953
supplied an intellectual pedigree running from Burke through John Adams to T. S. Eliot. William F. Buckley
Jr. founded National Review in 1955 as the movement's central publication, and used it to define boundaries
as much as to argue, notably by pushing the conspiracist John Birch Society and the militant atheist
individualism of Ayn Rand outside the coalition. Barry Goldwater's presidential candidacy in 1964 was
crushed at the polls but built the activist base that produced Ronald Reagan's victory in 1980.

Fusionism was the organising formula. Three constituencies with genuinely different priorities were joined
in one coalition: economic conservatives wanting low taxes, deregulation and free trade; social and
religious conservatives concerned with family, abortion, education and public morality; and
anti-communists, later national security hawks, wanting a large military and an assertive foreign policy.
Reagan's phrase for the arrangement, borrowed from the Eleventh Commandment about not speaking ill of fellow
Republicans, papered over real disagreements that only surfaced when the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.

Distinctively American features are worth noting because they do not travel. Federalism gives states genuine
authority, so conservative energy often flows into state legislatures and into constitutional arguments
about the limits of federal power. The Second Amendment makes firearms a constitutional rather than merely a
policy question. The absence of an established church, combined with very high religiosity, produced a
politics in which religious conservatism operates through voluntary mobilisation rather than through a state
church, which historians generally regard as making it more energetic rather than less. And the legacy of
slavery and segregation shaped party coalitions decisively: the Democratic Party's embrace of civil rights
legislation in the 1960s moved the white South toward the Republicans over the following decades, a
realignment whose causes historians continue to debate but whose fact is not in question.

sections.heading: Neoconservatism and the Foreign-Policy Question
sections.body:
Conservatism has no single foreign policy, and the disagreements within it on this subject are as deep as
any it contains. Three broad positions recur: realism, which judges foreign commitments by national interest
and is sceptical of moral crusades; non-interventionism, which holds that foreign entanglements corrupt
domestic liberty and drain resources; and interventionism, which holds that the character of other states
matters to security and that power should be used to shape the international order.

Neoconservatism is the best-known American form of the third position, and its origins are peculiar. Its
founders were largely former liberals and in some cases former socialists, mostly New York intellectuals,
who moved rightward from the 1960s in reaction to the counterculture, to the perceived failures of Great
Society welfare programmes, and to what they saw as a growing softness toward the Soviet Union. Irving
Kristol's much-quoted description of a neoconservative as a liberal who has been mugged by reality captures
the self-understanding. Their domestic disposition was not anti-government in the libertarian sense; many
accepted the welfare state's basic structure while attacking specific programmes as counterproductive, and
the journal The Public Interest, founded in 1965, specialised in showing that well-intentioned interventions
produced perverse results.

In foreign policy the position hardened into a claim that the character of regimes determines their
behaviour, that democracies do not fight one another, and that the United States should therefore actively
promote democratic government abroad, by force where necessary. This provided much of the intellectual
architecture for the invasion of Iraq in 2003. The subsequent course of that war, the absence of the weapons
stockpiles cited as justification, and the long insurgency discredited the position substantially, including
among many who had held it, and produced a significant revival of non-interventionist sentiment on the
American right.

The older non-interventionist strand had deep roots. George Washington's Farewell Address of 1796 warned
against permanent alliances, and the America First Committee opposed entry into the Second World War until
Pearl Harbor. That tradition, marginal during the Cold War, returned to prominence after 2016 in arguments
against foreign military commitments and against the assumption that trade liberalisation serves the
national interest.

Realism, associated with figures such as Hans Morgenthau, George Kennan and Henry Kissinger, holds the
middle ground and is arguably closest to the classical conservative temperament, since it emphasises limits,
unintended consequences and the intractability of other societies. Kennan, the architect of containment,
spent his later decades warning against precisely the moralised and militarised version of his doctrine that
others built. Which of these three positions counts as authentically conservative is not a question with an
answer; all three have been held by serious conservatives, and the disagreement is internal to the tradition
rather than a dispute about its boundaries.

sections.heading: Christian Democracy and Postwar Europe
sections.body:
The dominant conservative formation in continental Europe after 1945 was not the counter-revolutionary
tradition, which had been discredited by its entanglements with authoritarian regimes, but Christian
democracy. It is much less familiar to English-speaking readers than Anglo-American conservatism, and
misunderstanding it is a common source of confusion when comparing European and American politics.

Christian democracy drew on Catholic social teaching, a body of doctrine developed from Pope Leo XIII's
encyclical Rerum Novarum in 1891, which condemned both socialism and unrestrained capitalism and asserted
that workers had a right to a living wage and to form associations. Pius XI's Quadragesimo Anno of 1931
added the principle of subsidiarity. The resulting political programme accepted a substantial welfare
state, supported cooperation between employers and organised labour rather than class conflict, defended
the family and the church's role in education, and was strongly committed to European integration as a
means of making war between European states impossible.

Its founding figures shaped postwar Europe directly. Konrad Adenauer, Chancellor of West Germany from 1949
to 1963, led the Christian Democratic Union and presided over the Federal Republic's reconstruction and
integration into the West. Alcide De Gasperi in Italy and Robert Schuman in France were the other members
of the trio usually credited with launching European integration, and the Schuman Declaration of May 1950,
which proposed pooling coal and steel production, is the origin of what became the European Union. The
German economic model, the social market economy theorised by Alfred Müller-Armack and implemented by
Ludwig Erhard, is Christian democracy's most distinctive economic contribution: competitive markets
combined with strong social insurance, sectoral wage bargaining and worker representation on company boards
through codetermination.

An American conservative encountering this tradition will find much that seems left-wing: universal
healthcare, generous unemployment insurance, statutory worker representation, high taxation and enthusiasm
for supranational institutions. A European Christian democrat encountering American conservatism will find
the market individualism startling and the hostility to social insurance close to incomprehensible. Both
are recognisably conservative in their own contexts, which is strong evidence for the view that conservatism
is defined by its relationship to a particular inheritance rather than by a fixed policy content.

Christian democracy's position has weakened since the 1990s as religious observance in Europe has fallen
sharply and as its centrist positioning has been squeezed. Parties such as the German CDU, the Dutch CDA
and the Italian Christian Democrats, the last of which dissolved amid corruption investigations in 1994,
have lost votes to both liberal and national-populist competitors. Whether the tradition can be rebuilt on a
secular basis, given that its social doctrine was explicitly theological, is an open question that its own
theorists debate.

sections.heading: National Conservatism, Populism and the Current Realignment
sections.body:
Since roughly 2010 conservative politics across the democratic world has been reshaped by movements that
break with the market-liberal consensus of the preceding decades. The pattern is international: the vote to
leave the European Union in the United Kingdom in June 2016, Donald Trump's election in the United States
in November 2016, and the strength of parties in France, Italy, Hungary, Poland, Sweden and elsewhere that
combine cultural conservatism with economic positions their predecessors would have rejected.

The intellectual content is reasonably consistent even where the parties differ. It holds that the nation
is the primary political community and the proper unit of solidarity; that borders and immigration control
are central rather than peripheral questions; that free trade and offshoring have imposed real costs on
particular places and workers which aggregate growth statistics conceal; that large corporations,
universities, media and international bodies constitute an insufficiently accountable elite; and that
cultural questions of identity, family and national history matter more than marginal tax rates. Some
strands add explicit industrial policy, tariffs and family subsidies, which represent a substantial break
with the fusionist settlement.

The disagreements about how to characterise all this are genuine and not merely partisan. One reading holds
that this is conservatism returning to type after an unusual liberal interlude, since attachment to place,
nation and inherited culture is older in the tradition than enthusiasm for global markets, and that the
fusionist alliance was always a Cold War expedient. A second reading holds that it is populism rather than
conservatism, on the grounds that populism claims to speak for a unified authentic people against a corrupt
elite and is therefore majoritarian, whereas conservatism has classically defended constitutional limits,
independent institutions and the protection of minorities against majorities. On this reading the
willingness of some national-conservative governments to weaken judicial independence, as in Hungary and
Poland during the 2010s, is not a conservative act at all but the opposite of one. A third reading
emphasises material causes: the deindustrialisation of particular regions, the 2008 financial crisis and its
long aftermath, and rapid demographic change, arguing that the ideological content follows the economics.

The evidence does not currently adjudicate cleanly between these accounts, and any confident answer should
be treated with suspicion. What can be said descriptively is that the coalition that held from the 1970s to
the 2000s, uniting free markets, traditional morality and an assertive foreign policy, has come apart in
several countries; that the resulting formations are more economically interventionist and less
internationalist than their predecessors; and that a serious argument is under way within conservatism about
whether constitutional restraint or cultural restoration is the more fundamental commitment when the two
conflict. That argument is unresolved and its resolution will do much to determine what the word means a
generation from now.

sections.heading: Conservatism Beyond the West
sections.body:
Treating conservatism as a European invention exported elsewhere obscures a great deal. Every society with
a long institutional history has produced arguments for preserving it, and several of those arguments are
older than Burke and were developed with more philosophical elaboration.

Confucian political thought, systematised from the teachings of Kong Fuzi in the fifth century before the
common era and dominant in imperial China for two millennia, is conservative in a recognisable sense. It
grounds order in ritual propriety and in reciprocal duties within hierarchical relationships, treats the
family as the model for political authority, holds that rulers legitimate themselves through virtue and
performance rather than through consent, and regards the transmission of a classical canon as the core of
education. Its influence on political culture in China, Korea, Japan, Vietnam and Singapore remains
substantial. Lee Kuan Yew's arguments in the 1990s about Asian values, holding that social order and
collective welfare should take priority over individual rights claims, drew explicitly on this inheritance,
and were contested just as explicitly by Asian democrats who regarded the framing as a convenient defence of
incumbent power.

Islamic political thought contains an equally developed traditionalist strand, resting on the authority of
revealed law, the consensus of scholars and the practice of the early community. It is essential to
distinguish traditional religious conservatism, which defends established schools of jurisprudence and
customary practice, from twentieth-century Islamist movements, which are frequently revolutionary in method
and modernist in organisation, seeking to remake the state according to an ideological programme. Many
traditional scholars have opposed those movements precisely on conservative grounds.

Hindu, Japanese and African traditions each have comparable strands: defence of caste and inherited
religious practice in one case, of imperial continuity and Shinto observance in another, of customary law,
lineage and chieftaincy in many African polities where colonial and postcolonial states overlaid but never
replaced older structures.

Two general observations follow. First, conservatism outside the West often confronts a problem that
European conservatives did not face in the same form: the tradition to be conserved was disrupted by
colonial rule, so conservative politics becomes entangled with anti-colonial nationalism and with disputes
about which of several available pasts counts as authentic. That entanglement makes labels imported from
European political history fit badly.

Second, the label is frequently used carelessly by outside commentators to mean religiously observant, or
authoritarian, or simply opposed to Western liberal norms, and these are different things that do not
reliably travel together. A careful reader should ask, of any group described as conservative, what
specifically it seeks to conserve, by what authority, and against what alternative, rather than assuming
that the answers resemble those familiar from Britain or America.

sections.heading: Criticisms, Internal Tensions and Limits
sections.body:
Conservatism attracts serious objections, and a fair account must state them at their strongest rather than
in caricature. Several also come from within the tradition.

The oldest criticism is that conservatism has functioned historically as the defence of privilege dressed in
philosophical clothing. Its arguments about accumulated wisdom, unintended consequences and the fragility of
order were deployed against the abolition of slavery, against extending the vote beyond property owners,
against votes for women, against trade union rights, against desegregation and against decolonisation. In
each case the predicted catastrophe did not arrive and the reform is now defended by conservatives
themselves. The pattern is documented enough that it demands an answer, and the honest conservative answer
is that prudential arguments are contingent and can be wrong, which concedes that the disposition provides
no guarantee of being right.

Albert Hirschman analysed the recurring forms of the argument in The Rhetoric of Reaction in 1991,
identifying three theses that appear across two centuries of opposition to reform: perversity, that the
change will produce the opposite of its aim; futility, that it will change nothing; and jeopardy, that it
will endanger some previous achievement. His point was not that these are always false, since sometimes
they are true, but that their automatic deployment regardless of the case suggests rhetoric rather than
analysis.

A second criticism is the indeterminacy problem. If the principle is to conserve, what is to be conserved
when the inheritance contains contradictory elements, or when the recent past was itself revolutionary?
Conservatives in post-communist states faced exactly this and answered in incompatible ways. The
practical consequence is that conservatism cannot by itself decide the questions that matter most, and must
import substantive commitments from elsewhere, whether religious, national or liberal.

A third is that the tradition has no stable account of when change is warranted. Burke supported the
American Revolution and the Glorious Revolution while condemning the French one, and the criteria he offered
for distinguishing them are debated by scholars to this day.

The internal tensions are equally real. Free markets dissolve the communities traditionalists defend.
National sovereignty conflicts with international commerce. Populist majoritarianism conflicts with
constitutional restraint. Religious conservatism conflicts with secular libertarianism in the same
coalition. These are not failures of tidiness; they are substantive disagreements about ends.

What survives all this, and what even sympathetic critics tend to grant, is the epistemic core: complex
social arrangements encode information their participants cannot fully articulate, reforms have consequences
their designers do not foresee, institutions are easier to destroy than to build, and legitimacy depends on
continuity as well as on justification. Those claims are defensible on their own terms and are supported by
a good deal of unhappy twentieth-century experience. They establish a burden of proof and a case for
caution. They do not establish that any particular thing should be preserved, and treating them as if they
did is the characteristic failure of the tradition.

guides.title: Socialism
guides.summary: A full account of socialism as an idea and as a practice: its definitions and disputes, its origins, the Marxian analysis at its core, the calculation debate, its major branches from social democracy to anarchism to command planning, its record in government, and the criticisms and replies that continue to define the argument.

sections.heading: Defining a Contested Word
sections.body:
Socialism is a family of political and economic doctrines united by the claim that the means of producing goods and services should be owned or controlled collectively — by society, by the state, by workers, or by communities — rather than privately by individuals who hire labour for wages. Beyond that core, the word covers arrangements so different from one another that arguments conducted with it frequently talk past each other, and a reader needs to know from the outset that no single definition commands agreement.

The disputes are substantive rather than semantic. One concerns the object of collective control: is it the whole economy, or only "the commanding heights" of banking, energy, transport and heavy industry, or only natural monopolies? A second concerns the agent: the central state, regional government, workers in each enterprise, consumers in cooperatives, or society as an undifferentiated whole? A third concerns the mechanism of coordination: administrative planning, markets in which the firms happen to be collectively owned, or a moneyless system of direct allocation? A fourth concerns method: revolution or elections. A fifth concerns the endpoint: for Marx, socialism was a transitional stage after which the state itself would wither away into communism, whereas for most social democrats the mixed economy is not a waystation but the destination.

Because of this, several familiar oppositions are unreliable. "Socialism versus communism" is used one way by Marxists, for whom communism is the later, higher, stateless stage, and another way in Cold War popular usage, where socialism meant the milder Western welfare states and communism the Soviet bloc. "Socialism versus capitalism" implies a binary that no real economy has ever occupied: every developed country runs a mixed economy in which the state's share of GDP ranges from roughly 25 to over 55 per cent and where large sectors — usually roads, courts, defence, basic education and much of health care — are collectively provided as a matter of course.

It is also worth separating three things that are often conflated. Ownership concerns who holds legal title and residual claims. Control concerns who actually makes decisions, which regulation can shift without changing title. Distribution concerns who ends up with the output, which taxes and transfers can reshape without touching either. A country can have high redistribution with almost entirely private ownership, as Denmark broadly does, or state ownership with harshly unequal distribution, as several nominally socialist states have done. Programmes described as socialist have targeted all three levers in different combinations.

Finally, the word carries an enormous emotional charge that varies by country. In much of Europe, Latin America and India it names an ordinary parliamentary tradition with a century of governing experience. In the United States it has functioned since the early twentieth century largely as a term of political abuse, applied to policies that European conservatives take for granted. Understanding what someone means requires knowing which tradition and which country's usage they are drawing on.

sections.heading: Origins Before Marx: Utopians, Owenites and the Early Movement
sections.body:
The word socialisme appears in French around 1832 in the Saint-Simonian journal Le Globe and in English at roughly the same date among the followers of Robert Owen. The ideas are older. Communal ownership appears in Plato's Republic for the guardian class, in the early Christian community described in Acts, in monastic rules, in the sixteenth-century Anabaptist experiments at Münster, in Thomas More's Utopia of 1516, and in the Diggers led by Gerrard Winstanley who occupied St George's Hill in Surrey in 1649 and declared the earth a common treasury.

What made the nineteenth century different was industrialisation. Between roughly 1780 and 1850 in Britain, and later elsewhere, the factory system concentrated enormous numbers of propertyless wage workers in cities under conditions that shocked contemporary observers of every political stripe. Child labour from age six, working days of 14 to 16 hours, life expectancy in Manchester in the 1840s recorded at around 26 years for labourers against about 38 nationally, and periodic mass unemployment during trade slumps created a visible social question that older political vocabularies could not address.

Three figures dominate the early response, later labelled the utopian socialists by Friedrich Engels in his 1880 pamphlet Socialism: Utopian and Scientific — a label that was polemical and somewhat unfair. Henri de Saint-Simon (1760-1825) argued that society should be run by industrialists, engineers and scientists on rational, productive principles rather than by an idle aristocracy, and that the government of men would give way to the administration of things. Charles Fourier (1772-1837) designed elaborate cooperative communities called phalanstères, each of 1,620 people organised so that work matched individual passions; roughly 30 Fourierist communities were founded in the United States, almost all failing within a decade. Robert Owen (1771-1858), a genuinely successful mill-owner, ran New Lanark in Scotland with an eight-hour day and free schooling while turning a profit, then poured his fortune into New Harmony, Indiana, which collapsed in about two years.

Alongside these ran a more combative current. Pierre-Joseph Proudhon published What Is Property? in 1840, answering his own question with "property is theft" while defending small producers' possession against large accumulation, and became the founding figure of anarchism. Louis Blanc argued in 1839 for state-financed "social workshops" and coined the formula, later attributed to Marx, that society should draw "from each according to his abilities, to each according to his needs" — the phrase in fact originates with Blanc and earlier with Étienne-Gabriel Morelly.

The revolutions of 1848 across Europe, in which socialist demands appeared briefly in government in France before the June Days massacre, marked the movement's first entry into national politics and its first defeat. The immediate lesson drawn across the Continent was that moral appeal and model communities would not suffice against organised state power, and that whatever came next would need a theory of how existing society actually worked.

sections.heading: Marx and Engels: The Analysis That Reorganised the Movement
sections.body:
Karl Marx (1818-1883) and Friedrich Engels (1820-1895) did not invent socialism, and they were not the first to advocate collective ownership. Their contribution was a theory that claimed to explain why capitalism produced the misery its critics described, why it would generate the class capable of ending it, and why it would eventually fail on its own terms. That claim to scientific status — that socialism followed from an analysis of how the existing system works rather than from a moral blueprint — is what allowed Marxism to displace rival socialisms across most of the Continent by 1900.

The framework has several interlocking parts. Historical materialism holds that the way a society organises production — its "mode of production" — conditions its politics, law, religion and ideas. History moves through successive modes: primitive communism, ancient slave societies, feudalism, capitalism, and eventually socialism. Transitions occur when the productive forces available, meaning technology and human skill, outgrow the property relations that organise them, at which point the relations become "fetters" and are burst apart in a period of social revolution. This is a structural theory, not a moral one; Marx was frequently scathing about socialists who argued from justice.

Class is defined by relationship to the means of production, not by income or status. Under capitalism the bourgeoisie owns productive property; the proletariat owns nothing but its capacity to work and must sell it to live. This is a relation, not a ranking, and it generates antagonism structurally rather than through the malice of individual employers, most of whom Marx regarded as themselves compelled by competition.

The most influential single text remains The Communist Manifesto, written for the Communist League and published in February 1848, weeks before the revolutions broke out. Its opening claim that "the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles" and its closing appeal to the workers of all countries defined how the movement saw itself. Its ten-point programme is instructive because much of it now sounds unremarkable: a progressive income tax, abolition of inheritance, free public education, centralisation of credit and transport in state hands.

Capital, whose first volume appeared in 1867, is the analytical core, with volumes two and three assembled by Engels from Marx's notes after his death. It is a study of capitalism's internal logic, not a description of socialism; Marx wrote almost nothing about how a socialist economy would actually run, dismissing such exercises as "writing recipes for the cookshops of the future." That silence is not incidental. It left his successors with a powerful critique and almost no institutional design, and much of the twentieth century consists of attempts to fill the gap.

sections.heading: Value, Surplus and Crisis: The Mechanism of the Marxian Critique
sections.body:
The engine of Marx's economics is the labour theory of value, inherited from Adam Smith and David Ricardo and then turned against their conclusions. In this framework the value of a commodity is determined by the socially necessary labour time required to produce it under average conditions of skill and intensity. "Socially necessary" is doing real work in that sentence: a slow or incompetent producer does not thereby create more value, and a technological improvement that halves the labour needed halves the value of the product even for firms still using old methods.

The crucial move concerns labour power. Marx distinguishes labour, the activity, from labour power, the capacity to work that the worker sells. Like any commodity, labour power has a value equal to the labour time needed to reproduce it — the food, housing, training and family maintenance that keep a worker alive and replaceable. But its use value to the employer is that it can produce more value than it costs. If subsistence requires the equivalent of four hours of work and the working day is ten hours, six hours are surplus, appropriated by the owner. This surplus value, in Marx's account, is the sole source of profit, interest and rent, and it is extracted not by cheating but through an exchange in which the worker is paid the full market value of what is sold.

From this Marx derives several tendencies. The rate of surplus value can be raised by lengthening the working day (absolute surplus value) or by cheapening subsistence goods through productivity growth (relative surplus value), which explains capitalism's relentless technological dynamism. Competition drives firms to substitute machinery for labour, raising what Marx calls the organic composition of capital. Since only labour produces surplus, a rising ratio of machinery to labour implies a tendency for the rate of profit to fall, offset by countervailing factors including cheaper inputs, higher exploitation and foreign expansion. Crises of overproduction recur because the drive to accumulate outruns the purchasing power of workers whose wages are held down by that same drive.

The theory faces serious technical difficulties, which honest exposition should state. The transformation problem — converting labour values into observed market prices when profit rates equalise across industries of differing capital intensity — was identified by Marx himself in volume three and has never been resolved to general satisfaction, despite substantial literatures on both sides. Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk's critique of 1896 remains the standard statement of the objection. The marginalist revolution of the 1870s, associated with William Stanley Jevons, Carl Menger and Léon Walras, replaced labour-value theory in mainstream economics with subjective marginal utility, and virtually no academic economist today uses the labour theory of value as a price theory.

What has proved more durable is the underlying sociological insight: that the employment relation involves an asymmetry of power, that the intensity and length of work are contested, and that unemployment functions as a disciplining device. These claims are testable, are widely tested, and survive without the value theory.

sections.heading: The Socialist Calculation Debate
sections.body:
If a society abolishes private ownership of productive assets and therefore markets for them, how does it decide what to produce and by what methods? This is the single most important technical question ever posed to socialism, and the argument about it ran from 1920 to the present.

Ludwig von Mises opened it in a 1920 article, expanded into Socialism in 1922. His claim was not that planners would be lazy or corrupt but that rational calculation would be logically impossible. Choosing between two production methods requires comparing the value of the inputs they consume in alternative uses. That comparison requires prices for capital goods. Prices for capital goods emerge from competitive bidding by owners risking their own property. Abolish the ownership and you abolish the bidding, hence the prices, hence the possibility of knowing whether building a railway with steel and concrete costs society more or less than the alternatives. Production would proceed by guesswork.

The first reply came from Oskar Lange in 1936-37 and Abba Lerner, proposing "market socialism" or the competitive solution. A Central Planning Board would set prices by trial and error, instructing state managers to produce where marginal cost equals price and to minimise cost, then raise prices for goods in shortage and lower them for goods in surplus. Lange argued this replicated the Walrasian auctioneer of general equilibrium theory more faithfully than real capitalism, since the board could adjust without the waste of business cycles. For a generation this was widely regarded as having settled the matter in socialism's favour.

Friedrich Hayek reformulated the objection in a way that has worn far better, most influentially in "The Use of Knowledge in Society" (1945). His point was epistemological rather than computational. The knowledge required to run an economy is not a set of data waiting to be collected; it is dispersed, tacit, local and often unarticulated — the particular circumstances of time and place known only to the man on the spot, the hunch about a supplier, the sense that a machine is about to fail. Prices are not merely coordinating signals but a mechanism for economising on knowledge nobody possesses in full. A planning board cannot gather what nobody has written down, and much of it would not survive being written down. Hayek added a dynamic point: markets are a discovery procedure that generates new knowledge through competition, and a system that only allocates known resources efficiently misses what matters.

The computational strand has revived with modern technology. Advocates including Paul Cockshott and Allin Cottrell argued in the 1990s that input-output planning of an economy with millions of products is now tractable, since sparse-matrix iterative methods scale far better than solving the full system of simultaneous equations would suggest. Critics respond that the binding constraint was never arithmetic but the quality and honesty of the input data, and that preferences and technologies are not stable coefficients waiting to be measured. The debate is genuinely unresolved.

sections.heading: The Great Split: Reform, Revolution and 1914
sections.body:
By 1900 the socialist movement was large, disciplined and international. The German Social Democratic Party (SPD) was the model: founded in 1875, illegal under Bismarck's anti-socialist laws from 1878 to 1890, it nonetheless won 34.8 per cent of the vote and became the largest party in the Reichstag in 1912, with a million members, its own newspapers, choirs, cycling clubs and funeral societies. The Second International, founded in Paris in 1889, coordinated parties across Europe and beyond and made May Day an international workers' holiday.

Beneath the growth ran an unresolved contradiction. The party's formal Marxism predicted capitalist collapse and revolution; its actual practice was electoral, parliamentary and increasingly successful within the existing order. Eduard Bernstein confronted this directly in Evolutionary Socialism (1899), arguing from the statistics that Marx's predictions were failing — the middle classes were growing rather than being proletarianised, capital ownership was spreading through joint-stock companies, wages were rising and crises were not intensifying. He concluded that socialism should be pursued through incremental reform and that "the movement is everything, the final goal nothing." This "revisionism" was formally condemned by the SPD but described what the party in fact did.

Karl Kautsky held the orthodox centre: revolution was inevitable but should be awaited rather than provoked, and the party's task was to build strength. On the left, Rosa Luxemburg answered Bernstein in Reform or Revolution (1900), insisting reforms were valuable but could not accumulate into socialism because they left the property relation untouched. Vladimir Lenin, in What Is To Be Done? (1902), argued that workers left alone develop only "trade union consciousness" and that a disciplined vanguard party of professional revolutionaries was required — a claim about organisation that would define twentieth-century communism.

The break came in August 1914. The International had repeatedly resolved that workers would not fight one another in a capitalist war. On 4 August the SPD deputies voted for war credits; French, Austrian and British socialists did likewise. The internationalist commitment collapsed within days, and the movement never reunified. Those who opposed the war gathered at Zimmerwald in Switzerland in 1915 and formed the nucleus of a new movement.

The Russian Revolution of 1917 completed the rupture. After Lenin's Bolsheviks took power in October, the founding of the Third International (Comintern) in 1919 imposed twenty-one conditions on member parties, including expulsion of reformists and adoption of the Bolshevik model. Socialist parties across Europe split, in Germany with a bitterness compounded by the Social Democratic government's use of the Freikorps to crush the Spartacist rising in January 1919 and the murder of Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht. From that point socialism and communism were separate, hostile movements, and the enmity between them materially assisted the rise of fascism.

sections.heading: Social Democracy and the Construction of the Welfare State
sections.body:
The reformist branch became the most consequential socialist tradition by the simple measure of how many people have lived under governments it formed. Its method is electoral, its instruments are taxation, regulation, public services, macroeconomic management and collective bargaining, and its stated goal shifted over the twentieth century from replacing capitalism to civilising it.

Sweden supplies the paradigm. The Social Democratic Party governed almost continuously from 1932 to 1976 — 44 years, the longest democratic tenure of any party in the world. The Saltsjöbaden Agreement of 1938 between the trade union confederation LO and the employers' federation established a framework of centralised bargaining without state interference that lasted decades. The Rehn-Meidner model, formulated in 1951, deliberately combined solidaristic wage policy, meaning equal pay for equal work regardless of the employer's profitability, with active labour market policy to retrain workers displaced when unprofitable firms failed. The design pushed low-productivity firms out of business on purpose and moved workers into high-productivity ones, which is why Sweden combined compressed wages with rapid growth.

Britain's post-war settlement was more statist. The Attlee government elected in 1945 nationalised the Bank of England, coal, civil aviation, telecommunications, railways, road haulage, electricity, gas and steel — roughly 20 per cent of the economy — and founded the National Health Service in July 1948 on the principle of care free at the point of use, funded from general taxation. The Beveridge Report of 1942, which sold 600,000 copies, framed the programme as an attack on "five giants": want, disease, ignorance, squalor and idleness.

Germany's SPD formally abandoned Marxism at Bad Godesberg in 1959, accepting markets with the slogan "as much competition as possible, as much planning as necessary," and became a governing party. France's Parti Socialiste under François Mitterrand won in 1981 on a radical programme of nationalisations and reflation, then executed the "tournant de la rigueur" in 1983 when capital flight and franc devaluation forced a reversal — a widely cited demonstration of the constraints on national social democracy in an open economy.

The tradition's achievements are large and measurable. Between 1945 and 1975 Western European economies grew at 4 to 5 per cent annually, inequality fell to historic lows, and universal health coverage, pensions and education were established. Its difficulties emerged with the stagflation of the 1970s, when the Phillips curve trade-off broke down, and with capital mobility after the collapse of the Bretton Woods system in 1971-73, which made it harder to tax mobile capital or run independent monetary policy. The "Third Way" of Tony Blair and Gerhard Schröder in the late 1990s accepted much of the market-liberal settlement while retaining redistribution, a move its supporters call realism and its critics call capitulation. That argument is still live.

sections.heading: Marxism-Leninism and the Command Economy in Practice
sections.body:
The Soviet model is the most consequential socialist experiment by any measure, and any serious treatment must describe both what it built and what it cost, without softening either.

Its institutional core was the command economy, established after the New Economic Policy's partial market restoration was ended in 1928. Gosplan, the State Planning Committee, drew up five-year plans setting output targets for roughly 20,000 to 25,000 product categories at the aggregate level, disaggregated by ministries into millions of specific assignments. Prices were administratively set and did not clear markets. Enterprises were judged on physical output targets, which generated the model's most notorious pathologies: factories producing nails by weight made a few huge ones, factories judged by count made tiny useless ones, quality was neglected because it was unmeasured, and managers systematically understated capacity to secure achievable targets, a practice called the ratchet effect.

The achievements were nonetheless real. The USSR industrialised faster than any country had previously: industrial output multiplied several-fold in the 1930s while the West was in depression, urbanisation rose from about 18 per cent in 1926 to over 60 per cent by the 1980s, literacy went from roughly 40 per cent to near-universal, and the country produced the industrial base that defeated the Wehrmacht, launched Sputnik in 1957 and put Yuri Gagarin in orbit in 1961. Life expectancy roughly doubled between 1917 and the 1960s.

The costs were catastrophic. Forced collectivisation of agriculture from 1929 destroyed the peasant economy and produced famine in 1932-33 in which excess deaths are estimated at 5 to 7 million across the USSR, with roughly 3.5 to 5 million in Ukraine, where the Holodomor is recognised by many states as genocide. The Great Terror of 1937-38 executed approximately 680,000 people according to NKVD records opened after 1991. The Gulag system held around 1.5 to 2.5 million prisoners at its peak in the early 1950s, with total deaths in the camps generally estimated between 1.5 and 1.8 million. China's Great Leap Forward from 1958 to 1962 produced a famine with credible death estimates ranging from 15 to 45 million, the deadliest in recorded history. Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge from 1975 to 1979 killed perhaps 1.5 to 2 million out of a population of 8 million.

Whether these outcomes follow from socialism as such or from the specific combination of one-party dictatorship, war, backwardness and terror is the central historical dispute. Anti-communist writers, including Hayek in The Road to Serfdom (1944), argued that comprehensive planning requires suppressing dissent because plans cannot survive democratic revision. Democratic socialists reply that the movement's own members were among the first victims, that social democracies achieved comparable growth without terror, and that no theoretical link runs from public ownership to mass killing. Both positions have serious advocates and the question is not settled by assertion.

sections.heading: Anarchism, Syndicalism and the Libertarian Left
sections.body:
A substantial socialist tradition rejected the state entirely, holding that the coercive apparatus of government could not be an instrument of liberation because it reproduces domination whoever holds it. This tradition lost the argument organisationally in the nineteenth century and has periodically returned.

Mikhail Bakunin (1814-1876) was Marx's principal antagonist in the First International, expelled at the Hague Congress of 1872 in a split that destroyed the organisation. Bakunin's prediction is much quoted because it reads as prophetic: a "dictatorship of the proletariat" would become a dictatorship over the proletariat by a new class of ex-workers turned rulers, "the most vile and terrible lie our century has created." Peter Kropotkin (1842-1921), a Russian prince turned geographer, supplied the constructive theory in The Conquest of Bread (1892) and Mutual Aid (1902), the latter arguing from field zoology that cooperation is at least as important an evolutionary factor as competition.

Anarcho-syndicalism made the trade union rather than the party the vehicle. The strategy was to build revolutionary unions capable of running industry, then seize it through a general strike. Its high point was Spain, where the Confederación Nacional del Trabajo reached over a million members by 1936. During the Civil War, following the July 1936 coup, workers in Catalonia and Aragon collectivised roughly 70 per cent of the workforce in Barcelona, running trams, telephones, textile mills and much of agriculture through assemblies and elected committees. George Orwell's Homage to Catalonia describes it from inside. The collectives functioned for two to three years under wartime conditions, then were destroyed by Franco's victory in 1939 and, earlier, suppressed by Communist forces in the May Days of 1937 in Barcelona. Historians disagree sharply about their economic performance, and the wartime setting makes clean judgement impossible.

Council communism, associated with Anton Pannekoek and Herman Gorter, proposed workers' councils — soviets in the original, pre-Bolshevik sense — as the organ of both revolution and government, rejecting both parliaments and vanguard parties.
